q: Cash from operations differs from funds from operations mainly because cash from operations is arrived at after adjusting funds from operations for:

options.A: Depreciation charged during the year only
options.B: Profit or loss on sale of fixed assets only
options.C: Changes in current assets other than cash and in current liabilities, such as debtors, stock and creditors
options.D: Income-tax paid during the year only

e: Funds from operations is based on working capital; to get cash from operations it is adjusted for changes in non-cash current assets and current liabilities like debtors, stock and creditors.

q: Net working capital represents the portion of current assets that is financed by:

options.A: Long-term sources of funds
options.B: Trade creditors only
options.C: Short-term bank borrowings only
options.D: Current liabilities

e: Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities; this excess of current assets is necessarily financed by long-term sources, since current liabilities finance only the remaining part.

q: Other things being equal, an enterprise with a longer production or manufacturing cycle will require:

options.A: Less working capital than an enterprise with a shorter cycle
options.B: No working capital at all
options.C: More working capital, because funds remain locked up for a longer period in work-in-progress
options.D: The same working capital irrespective of the cycle length

e: A longer production cycle keeps funds locked in work-in-progress and finished stock for more time before sale and collection, so the enterprise needs more working capital.

q: Which of the following will tend to reduce the working capital requirement of an enterprise?

options.A: Prompt collection from debtors and faster turnover of inventory
options.B: A liberal credit policy allowing customers longer time to pay
options.C: Longer storage of raw materials before use in production
options.D: A large seasonal peak in production and sales

e: Prompt collection from debtors and faster inventory turnover shorten the time funds stay blocked, directly reducing the working capital requirement; the other options lengthen the blocking period.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 9,50,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 4,50,000. Its net working capital is:
e: Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = 9,50,000 - 4,50,000 = Rs 5,00,000.

q: An enterprise has stock of Rs 2,00,000, debtors of Rs 1,50,000 and cash of Rs 50,000 as its only current assets. Its gross working capital is:
e: Gross working capital is the total of all current assets = Stock 2,00,000 + Debtors 1,50,000 + Cash 50,000 = Rs 4,00,000.

q: Raw materials are held for 40 days, the production process takes 20 days, finished goods are held for 25 days and debtors are collected in 50 days. Creditors allow 35 days' credit. The length of the operating cycle is:

options.A: 135 days
options.B: 100 days
options.C: 85 days
options.D: 115 days

e: Operating cycle = 40 + 20 + 25 + 50 - Creditors 35 = 135 - 35 = 100 days, the net period for which funds remain blocked in operations.

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 36,50,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its operating cycle is 50 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = Annual operating cost / 365 x Operating cycle = 36,50,000 / 365 x 50 = 10,000 x 50 = Rs 5,00,000.

q: A public utility undertaking generally needs relatively less working capital mainly because:

options.A: It renders services largely for cash and does not carry large inventories of finished goods
options.B: It incurs no operating expenses
options.C: It purchases all its materials only for cash
options.D: Its production cycle is the longest among all industries

e: A public utility sells services largely for cash and holds little finished-goods inventory, so funds are blocked only briefly and its working capital need is relatively low.

q: PERT was originally developed in 1958 for:

options.A: Scheduling the construction of a chemical plant by DuPont
options.B: Preparing the annual railway budget
options.C: The Polaris missile programme of the US Navy
options.D: Controlling inventory in a manufacturing concern

e: PERT was developed in 1958 by the US Navy for planning and controlling the Polaris missile programme, a research project with uncertain activity times.

q: CPM was originally developed by DuPont primarily for:

options.A: Appraising the return on a new railway line
options.B: Fixing freight rates for goods traffic
options.C: Analysing variances in standard costing
options.D: Scheduling and controlling construction and plant maintenance projects where activity times are fairly predictable

e: CPM was developed by DuPont for scheduling construction and plant maintenance projects where activity durations are fairly predictable from experience, enabling cost-time analysis.

q: The correct distinction between PERT and CPM as regards orientation is:

options.A: PERT is activity-oriented and CPM is event-oriented
options.B: Both PERT and CPM are event-oriented
options.C: PERT is event-oriented and CPM is activity-oriented
options.D: Both PERT and CPM are activity-oriented

e: PERT is event-oriented, focusing on milestones or events in projects with uncertain times, while CPM is activity-oriented, focusing on activities with known times.

q: In PERT, an activity has an optimistic time of 8 days, a most likely time of 14 days and a pessimistic time of 26 days. Its expected time is:

options.A: 14 days
options.B: 15 days
options.C: 16 days
options.D: 18 days

e: Expected time = (Optimistic + 4 x Most likely + Pessimistic) / 6 = (8 + 4 x 14 + 26) / 6 = 90 / 6 = 15 days.

q: In PERT, an activity has an optimistic time of 4 days, a most likely time of 13 days and a pessimistic time of 16 days. Its expected time is:

options.A: 12 days
options.B: 11 days
options.C: 13 days
options.D: 10 days

q: In PERT, the optimistic time of an activity is 7 days and the pessimistic time is 19 days. The standard deviation of the activity time, computed as (TP - TO) / 6, is:

options.A: 2 days
options.B: 4 days
options.C: 6 days
options.D: 12 days

e: Standard deviation = (Pessimistic - Optimistic) / 6 = (19 - 7) / 6 = 12 / 6 = 2 days.

q: As compared to PERT, CPM places greater emphasis on:

options.A: The probability of completing the project by a given date
options.B: The use of three time estimates for each activity
options.C: The sequencing of events in a research project
options.D: Optimising project cost by balancing direct cost against project time, that is, the cost-time trade-off

e: CPM emphasises the cost-time trade-off - crashing activities at extra cost to shorten project duration optimally - whereas PERT emphasises time probability in uncertain research projects.

q: A key limitation of sensitivity analysis in project appraisal is that it:

options.A: Cannot be used with the Discounted Cash Flow technique
options.B: Always requires the cost of capital as an input
options.C: Varies one variable at a time assuming the other variables remain unchanged, thus ignoring inter-relationships between variables and the probability of the change occurring
options.D: Considers only the payback period of the project

e: Sensitivity analysis changes one variable at a time holding others constant, so it ignores inter-relationships between variables and gives no probability for the changes examined.

q: In project appraisal, sensitivity analysis mainly helps management to:

options.A: Guarantee the projected rate of return of the project
options.B: Identify the critical variables to whose changes the project's return is most sensitive, so that they can be estimated carefully and monitored closely
options.C: Eliminate all risk from the project
options.D: Fix the discount rate to be used in appraisal

e: Sensitivity analysis shows which variables most affect the project's return, identifying critical variables that management must estimate carefully and monitor closely during execution.

q: A controllable variance is a variance:

options.A: Which arises wholly from external factors beyond anyone's control
options.B: Which is always favourable to the enterprise
options.C: For which a specific manager or department can be held responsible, because it arises from factors within their control
options.D: Which is too small to be investigated

e: A controllable variance arises from factors within a specific manager's or department's control, so that manager can fairly be held responsible for it.

q: The fixed overhead capacity variance arises due to the difference between:

options.A: Budgeted fixed overheads and actual fixed overheads incurred
options.B: Budgeted hours of work and actual hours worked, valued at the standard fixed overhead rate
options.C: Standard output and actual output in units only
options.D: Budgeted variable overheads and actual variable overheads

e: Fixed overhead capacity variance = (Budgeted hours - Actual hours) x Standard fixed overhead rate; it arises when the capacity provided is used for more or fewer hours than budgeted.

q: A favourable material price variance should not automatically be regarded as good performance because it may have been achieved by:

options.A: Negotiating a genuine and lasting reduction in price
options.B: Purchasing materials in economic order quantities
options.C: Paying suppliers promptly to earn cash discount
options.D: Buying inferior quality material, which may cause an adverse usage variance and production problems

e: A favourable price variance may simply reflect buying inferior quality material, which then causes excess consumption, wastage and an adverse usage variance - so it is not automatically good performance.

q: A finance lease is distinguished from an operating lease in that a finance lease:

options.A: Transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership to the lessee and generally covers a major part of the asset's economic life
options.B: Is always cancellable by the lessee at short notice without penalty
options.C: Covers only a small fraction of the asset's economic life
options.D: Leaves all risks of ownership with the lessor throughout

e: A finance lease transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership to the lessee and usually runs for a major part of the asset's economic life, unlike a short, cancellable operating lease.

q: The lease rentals payable by Indian Railways to IRFC for rolling stock leased to it essentially comprise:

options.A: Only the dividend on the capital-at-charge
options.B: Recovery of the principal, that is the capital component, and interest on the funds raised for that stock
options.C: Only the maintenance cost of the rolling stock
options.D: Only the depreciation charge of the rolling stock

e: Lease rentals paid to IRFC comprise the capital component, recovering the principal cost of the rolling stock, plus interest on the funds IRFC raised to acquire it.

q: Extra Budgetary Resources through Institutional Finance, EBR(IF), are raised mainly to finance:

options.A: Remunerative projects and acquisition of rolling stock that can service the debt from their earnings
options.B: Day-to-day establishment and pension payments
options.C: Routine repairs and maintenance of track
options.D: Only unremunerative passenger amenity works

e: EBR(IF) is institutional borrowing raised for remunerative projects and rolling stock acquisition whose earnings can service the debt, not for day-to-day revenue expenditure.

q: Lease financing enables the Railways to acquire rolling stock:

options.A: Free of cost from the leasing company
options.B: Without paying any rental during the lease period
options.C: Without meeting the entire capital cost upfront from budgetary resources, the payment being spread as lease rentals over the life of the asset
options.D: Without any liability being recorded for the lease rentals

e: Lease financing spreads the payment for rolling stock as rentals over the asset's life, so the Railways acquire it without bearing the entire capital cost upfront from budgetary resources.

q: In PPP terminology, DBFOT stands for:

options.A: Design, Build, Fund, Own and Transfer
options.B: Develop, Build, Finance, Own and Transfer
options.C: Design, Bid, Finance, Operate and Terminate
options.D: Design, Build, Finance, Operate and Transfer

e: DBFOT stands for Design, Build, Finance, Operate and Transfer - the private partner designs, builds, finances and operates the facility during the concession and then transfers it back.

q: Under the Viability Gap Funding scheme for PPP projects, the Central Government may provide up to 20% of the total project cost and the sponsoring authority up to a further 20%. The maximum total Viability Gap Funding is therefore:

options.A: 20% of the total project cost
options.B: 25% of the total project cost
options.C: 30% of the total project cost
options.D: 40% of the total project cost

e: Maximum VGF = Central Government 20% + Sponsoring authority 20% = 40% of the total project cost.

q: In a PPP project, the concession agreement is the agreement between:

options.A: The SPV and its lenders only
options.B: The main contractor and its sub-contractors
options.C: The government authority granting the concession and the SPV or concessionaire, giving it the right to build and operate the facility for the concession period
options.D: The SPV and the users of the facility

e: The concession agreement is between the government authority granting the concession and the SPV or concessionaire, authorising it to build and operate the facility for the concession period.

q: A basic principle of risk allocation in PPP projects is that each risk should be allocated to:

options.A: The party best able to manage and bear that risk at the least cost
options.B: The government in every case
options.C: The private partner in every case
options.D: The lenders financing the project in every case

e: Efficient PPP risk allocation assigns each risk to the party best able to manage and bear it at least cost, rather than loading all risks on either the government or the private partner.

q: In IRPSM, proposals for new works in the Works Programme are initiated and processed by:

options.A: Contractors executing railway works
options.B: Field units, divisions and zonal railways, which feed the proposals online for examination and prioritisation
options.C: The Comptroller and Auditor General
options.D: Passengers and freight customers

e: In IRPSM, work proposals originate from field units, divisions and zonal railways, which feed them online for examination, finance scrutiny and prioritisation.

q: IRPSM assists in capital budgeting and appraisal mainly by providing:

options.A: A system for fixing tariffs and freight rates
options.B: A system for collecting cash earnings at stations
options.C: A common online platform for examination, finance scrutiny, prioritisation within the budget ceiling and inclusion of proposals in the Pink Book
options.D: A system for conducting the statutory audit of works

e: IRPSM provides a common online platform for examination, finance scrutiny and prioritisation of works proposals within the budget ceiling, and for their inclusion in the Pink Book.

q: After a work is sanctioned, IRPSM is used for:

options.A: Monitoring its physical and financial progress, expenditure and milestones against the sanction
options.B: Fixing the pay of staff posted on the work
options.C: Selling surplus materials arising from the work
options.D: Preparing the personal claims of officers supervising the work

e: After sanction, IRPSM tracks the work's physical and financial progress, expenditure and milestones against the sanctioned scope and cost.

q: In traffic costing, the cost of a traffic service is broadly analysed into:

options.A: Fixed costs and period costs only
options.B: Terminal costs and line-haul or movement costs
options.C: Fuel costs and staff costs only
options.D: Capital costs and dividend payable on capital

e: Traffic costing broadly divides service cost into terminal costs, incurred at originating and destination terminals, and line-haul or movement costs, incurred in hauling traffic between them.

q: Specific Energy Consumption for electric traction in railway costing is generally expressed as energy consumed per:

options.A: 100 Net Tonne Kilometres
options.B: 1000 Passenger Kilometres
options.C: Wagon day
options.D: 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres

e: Specific Energy Consumption for electric traction is expressed as energy consumed per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres, relating energy use to the gross load hauled including the vehicle weight.

q: Pricing a traffic service strictly on its fully distributed cost may lead to loss of otherwise remunerative traffic because:

options.A: A service that does not cover its fully distributed cost may still make a positive contribution if its earnings exceed the incremental or marginal cost of carrying it
options.B: Fully distributed cost includes no share of overheads at all
options.C: Marginal cost is always higher than fully distributed cost
options.D: Fully distributed cost is based only on fuel consumption

e: A service failing to cover fully distributed cost may still earn more than its incremental cost and thus make a positive contribution; pricing it out on fully distributed cost would lose that contribution.

q: A cost is classified as a direct cost of a particular job when it:

options.A: Is incurred for the factory as a whole
options.B: Remains fixed in total at all levels of output
options.C: Can be economically identified with and traced to that job in full
options.D: Is apportioned to the job on the basis of floor area

e: A direct cost can be economically identified with and traced in full to a particular job, unlike indirect costs which are common to many jobs and must be apportioned.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Product costs are inventoried and carried forward as part of the value of stock until the goods are sold.
2. Period costs are charged in full against the revenue of the period in which they are incurred.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements are correct: product costs are inventoried in stock values until sale, while period costs are charged in full against the revenue of the period in which they are incurred.

q: The salary of a factory manager who supervises several jobs, none of which can claim his time exclusively, is treated in the cost of an individual job as:

options.A: An indirect labour cost recovered through factory overheads
options.B: A direct labour cost of the largest job
options.C: A direct expense of every job in full
options.D: A selling overhead of the job

e: The factory manager's salary serves many jobs and cannot be traced to any one job, so for an individual job it is indirect labour recovered through factory overheads.

q: Discretionary (managed) fixed costs are distinguished from committed fixed costs in that discretionary fixed costs:

options.A: Arise from owning plant and long-term leases
options.B: Cannot be altered even over several years
options.C: Vary in direct proportion to output
options.D: Arise from periodic management decisions, such as research and publicity outlays, and can be curtailed without immediately impairing capacity

e: Discretionary fixed costs arise from periodic management decisions like research and publicity and can be cut without immediately impairing operating capacity, unlike committed costs from owning plant or long leases.

q: In a cost sheet, administration overheads are added after arriving at:

options.A: Prime cost
options.B: Works (factory) cost, to arrive at the cost of production
options.C: Cost of sales, to arrive at the selling price
options.D: Direct material cost only

e: In a cost sheet, works (factory) cost plus administration overheads gives the cost of production; prime cost comes earlier and selling overheads are added later to get cost of sales.

q: When output rises within the existing capacity, the behaviour of costs is best stated as:

options.A: Total variable cost rises, variable cost per unit stays constant, and fixed cost per unit falls
options.B: Total variable cost stays constant and fixed cost per unit rises
options.C: Both fixed and variable costs per unit rise
options.D: Total fixed cost rises in proportion to output

e: When output rises within capacity, total variable cost rises but variable cost per unit stays constant, while total fixed cost is unchanged so fixed cost per unit falls.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 8,000 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 40 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:

options.A: 200 units
options.B: 283 units
options.C: 400 units
options.D: 800 units

e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x Annual consumption x Ordering cost / Carrying cost) = sqrt(2 x 8,000 x 40 / 4) = sqrt(1,60,000) = 400 units.

q: The minimum stock level of a material is fixed primarily to ensure that:

options.A: The maximum possible quantity is always held in stores
options.B: Production does not come to a halt during the lead time, after allowing for normal consumption in that period
options.C: The re-order quantity is fully consumed before the next order
options.D: Obsolete stock can be disposed of quickly

e: The minimum stock level is a safety buffer ensuring production does not halt during the lead time, covering normal consumption in that period plus a margin for delays.

q: In a period of steadily rising material prices, valuing issues under FIFO, as compared to the weighted average method, will generally result in:

options.A: A higher charge to production and a lower value of closing stock
options.B: No difference in either charge or stock value
options.C: Issues priced at the latest prices in both methods
options.D: A lower charge to production and a higher value of closing stock, because the earliest (cheaper) lots are charged out first

e: Under FIFO the earliest, cheapest lots are charged to production first when prices are rising, so the charge to production is lower and closing stock, valued at recent higher prices, is higher than under weighted average.

q: A favourable material price variance accompanied by an adverse material usage variance most commonly suggests that:

options.A: Cheaper, inferior material was bought, causing excess consumption and wastage in production
options.B: Material prices fell in the market without any action by the buyer
options.C: Workers used the material more carefully than the standard
options.D: The standard price was set too low by mistake

e: Cheap but inferior material explains this combination: it lowers purchase price (favourable price variance) but causes excess consumption and wastage, producing an adverse usage variance.

q: A worker is allowed 12 hours for a job and completes it in 9 hours at a wage rate of Rs 60 per hour. His total earnings under the Halsey premium bonus plan (50% of time saved) are:

options.A: Rs 630
options.B: Rs 540
options.C: Rs 720
options.D: Rs 600

e: Time saved = 12 - 9 = 3 hours. Earnings = Time taken wages 9 x 60 = Rs 540 plus bonus 50% of time saved wages 0.5 x 3 x 60 = Rs 90, total Rs 630.

q: The Rowan premium bonus plan differs from the Halsey plan in that under the Rowan plan the bonus is:

options.A: A fixed 50% of the wages of time saved in all cases
options.B: The proportion of time saved to time allowed, applied to the wages of the time taken, so that the bonus increases at a diminishing rate as time saved grows
options.C: Paid only when output exceeds twice the standard
options.D: Paid in kind and not in cash

e: Under Rowan, bonus = (Time saved / Time allowed) x Wages of time taken, so the worker's share of the saving falls proportionately as more time is saved and the bonus grows at a diminishing rate.

q: A high rate of labour turnover in a factory most directly leads to:

options.A: Lower recruitment and training costs
options.B: Higher selection, training and learning-period costs and lower productivity of new workers
options.C: An automatic reduction in factory overheads
options.D: Elimination of idle time in production

e: High labour turnover raises selection, recruitment and training costs and lowers productivity during new workers' learning period, besides disrupting production.

q: In computing a machine hour rate, depreciation of the machine and its insurance premium are treated as:

options.A: Running charges varying with the hours worked
options.B: Direct expenses of each job done on the machine
options.C: Selling overheads of the factory
options.D: Standing charges, spread over the working hours of the machine

e: Depreciation and insurance do not vary with hours worked; they are standing charges of the machine, spread over its working hours in computing the machine hour rate, unlike running charges like power.

q: Budgeted factory overheads are Rs 3,60,000 and the budgeted labour hours are 60,000, giving the absorption rate. Actual labour hours worked are 58,000 and actual overheads incurred are Rs 3,60,000. The overheads are:

options.A: Under-absorbed by Rs 12,000
options.B: Over-absorbed by Rs 12,000
options.C: Exactly absorbed
options.D: Under-absorbed by Rs 2,000

e: Absorption rate = 3,60,000 / 60,000 hours = Rs 6 per hour. Absorbed overheads = 58,000 x 6 = Rs 3,48,000 against actual Rs 3,60,000, so overheads are under-absorbed by Rs 12,000.

q: A single blanket overhead absorption rate for the whole factory is most suitable when:

options.A: The factory has many departments doing very different work
options.B: The factory produces a single product, or all products pass through all departments in the same proportion
options.C: Each department uses a different absorption base
options.D: Service departments dominate the factory costs

e: A blanket rate uses one factory-wide rate, so it is fair only when there is a single product or all products use all departments in the same proportion; with diverse departments it distorts product costs.

q: Where the amount of under-absorbed overhead is small and arises from normal estimation differences, it is generally disposed of by:

options.A: Carrying it forward indefinitely as an asset
options.B: Adding it to the cost of the next year's production only
options.C: Transferring it to the Costing Profit and Loss Account of the period
options.D: Recovering it from the workers of the department

e: Small under-absorption from normal estimation differences is not material enough for a supplementary rate, so it is written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account of the period.

q: For apportioning the rent of a factory building among its departments in primary distribution, the most equitable basis is generally the:

options.A: Number of workers in each department
options.B: Direct wages paid in each department
options.C: Value of machinery in each department
options.D: Floor area occupied by each department

e: Rent is an occupancy cost driven by space used, so primary apportionment on floor area occupied by each department is the most equitable basis.

q: In a process, 2,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 91,000. Normal loss is 10% of input and the scrap realises Rs 5 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
e: Normal loss is 10 percent of 2,000 = 200 units, scrap recovery is 200 x Rs 5 = Rs 1,000, so cost per good unit = (91,000 - 1,000) / 1,800 = Rs 50.00.

q: In process costing, where the actual loss in a process is less than the normal loss, the abnormal gain so arising is:

options.A: Valued at scrap value only and ignored in the process account
options.B: Valued at the cost per unit of good output, with the scrap value of the shortfall in scrap adjusted against it
options.C: Credited to the general Profit and Loss Account at selling price
options.D: Added to the input cost of the next process

e: Abnormal gain is valued at the normal cost per unit of good output, not scrap value, and the scrap value forgone on the units saved is debited against it so only the net gain is credited.

q: A joint cost of Rs 90,000 is apportioned between Products A and B on the physical units basis. Output of A is 600 units and of B is 300 units. The share of joint cost borne by A is:
e: On the physical units basis, A share = 600 / (600 + 300) x Rs 90,000 = 600/900 x 90,000 = Rs 60,000.

q: Where a by-product has a regular market and its sales value is material, a commonly accepted treatment is to:

options.A: Credit its net realisable value to the process account, reducing the cost borne by the main product
options.B: Charge its full joint cost to the main product in addition
options.C: Record it only in a memorandum register with no cost effect
options.D: Treat it as the main product of the process

e: When a by-product has a material realisable value, crediting its net realisable value to the process account reduces the joint cost borne by the main product and matches value recovered.

q: The annual demand for a component is 10,000 units. The set-up cost per batch is Rs 200 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EBQ = sqrt(2DS/C), the Economic Batch Quantity is:

options.A: 500 units
options.B: 2,000 units
options.C: 1,414 units
options.D: 1,000 units

e: EBQ = sqrt(2 x 10,000 x 200 / 4) = sqrt(1,000,000) = 1,000 units, where set-up cost and carrying cost are equal.

q: In job costing, the document that accumulates the material, labour and overhead cost of one specific job from start to completion is the:

options.A: Bin card of the stores
options.B: Time card of a worker
options.C: Job cost card (job cost sheet) maintained for that job number
options.D: General ledger control account

e: The job cost card or sheet opened for each job number accumulates its direct material, direct labour and absorbed overheads from start to completion to give total job cost.

q: A product sells for Rs 250 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 175 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 4,50,000. The break-even sales value is:
e: Contribution is Rs 250 - Rs 175 = Rs 75 and P/V ratio is 75/250 = 30 percent, so break-even sales = 4,50,000 / 0.30 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 20,00,000, its P/V ratio is 35% and its fixed costs are Rs 4,20,000. Its margin of safety in sales value is:
An enterprise wants to earn a profit after tax of Rs 90,000. The tax rate is 25%, fixed costs are Rs 2,80,000 and the P/V ratio is 40%. The sales required are:
A high degree of operating leverage in a firm implies that, other things being equal:

options.A: Its operating profit is highly sensitive to changes in sales volume, rising sharply when sales rise and falling sharply when sales fall
options.B: Its operating profit does not change with sales at all
options.C: It has no fixed costs in its cost structure
options.D: Its business risk is the lowest possible

e: Operating leverage is high when fixed costs form a large share of total cost, so a small change in sales produces a magnified change in operating profit in either direction.

q: A firm sells two products: P with sales of Rs 5,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 50%, and Q with sales of Rs 5,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 30%. Total fixed costs are Rs 3,20,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:
e: Total contribution = 5,00,000 x 50 percent + 5,00,000 x 30 percent = Rs 4,00,000 on sales of Rs 10,00,000, giving weighted P/V of 40 percent, so break-even sales = 3,20,000 / 0.40 = Rs 8,00,000.

q: Where a single scarce resource limits the output of several products, the product mix that maximises total profit is obtained by ranking the products according to:

options.A: Selling price per unit, highest first
options.B: Contribution per unit of the scarce resource consumed
options.C: Total sales value of each product
options.D: Variable cost per unit, lowest first

e: With one limiting factor, profit is maximised by ranking products on contribution per unit of the scarce resource used, not on selling price or contribution per unit alone.

q: Fixed costs of a factory are Rs 3,00,000, which include depreciation of Rs 60,000. The P/V ratio is 30%. The cash break-even sales are:
e: Cash fixed cost excludes non-cash depreciation, so it is 3,00,000 - 60,000 = Rs 2,40,000, and cash break-even sales = 2,40,000 / 0.30 = Rs 8,00,000.

q: Fixed production overheads of a factory are Rs 90,000. Production during the period is 15,000 units and sales are 13,000 units. Compared with marginal costing, the profit under absorption costing will be:

options.A: Higher by Rs 12,000
options.B: Lower by Rs 12,000
options.C: Higher by Rs 18,000
options.D: Exactly the same

e: Fixed overhead rate = 90,000 / 15,000 = Rs 6 per unit; 2,000 unsold units (15,000 - 13,000) carry Rs 12,000 in closing stock under absorption costing, so its profit is higher by Rs 12,000.

q: A semi-variable cost can be segregated into its fixed and variable elements for budgeting and control by using, among others:

options.A: The sales value method
options.B: The physical units method
options.C: The high-low method, comparing total cost at the highest and lowest levels of activity
options.D: The market price method

e: The high-low method takes total cost at the highest and lowest activity levels; the difference divided by the difference in activity gives the variable rate, leaving the fixed element.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 4,50,000 per year, of which Rs 1,50,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. The contribution is Rs 50 per unit. The shutdown point is:

options.A: 9,000 units
options.B: 3,000 units
options.C: 7,500 units
options.D: 6,000 units

e: Avoidable fixed cost = 4,50,000 - 1,50,000 = Rs 3,00,000, so shutdown point = 3,00,000 / Rs 50 contribution = 6,000 units; below this, shutting down loses less.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 30 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 28 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 4,000 kg. The material price variance is:

options.A: Rs 8,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 2,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 8,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 1,12,000 (Favourable)

e: Material price variance = (Standard price - Actual price) x Actual quantity = (30 - 28) x 4,000 = Rs 8,000 Favourable, since actual price is lower.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 2,500 hours, but only 2,300 hours were actually taken. The standard rate is Rs 40 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 8,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 8,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 9,200 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 2,00,000 (Favourable)

e: Labour efficiency variance = (Standard hours - Actual hours) x Standard rate = (2,500 - 2,300) x Rs 40 = Rs 8,000 Favourable, as less time was taken.

q: The budgeted production of a factory is 12,000 units and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 5 per unit. Actual production is 10,500 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:

options.A: Rs 7,500 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 52,500 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 7,500 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 1,500 (Adverse)

e: Fixed overhead volume variance = (Actual production - Budgeted production) x Standard rate = (10,500 - 12,000) x Rs 5 = Rs 7,500 Adverse, due to under-production.

q: The variable overhead variance of a department is best analysed by comparing the actual variable overheads incurred with:

options.A: The budgeted fixed overheads of the factory
options.B: The variable overheads absorbed on the basis of actual hours only
options.C: The profit of the previous period
options.D: The flexed allowance — standard hours for actual output multiplied by the standard variable overhead rate — together with the spending on actual hours

e: Variable overhead variance is split by comparing actual spend with the allowance on actual hours for spending, and the allowance on actual hours with standard hours for actual output at the standard rate for efficiency.

q: The standard mix for a batch of 100 kg is: Material X — 50 kg at Rs 12 per kg, Material Y — 50 kg at Rs 8 per kg. The actual mix used for a 100 kg batch is X — 40 kg and Y — 60 kg. The material mix variance is:

options.A: Rs 40 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 40 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 200 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 100 (Adverse)

e: At standard prices, standard mix costs 50 x 12 + 50 x 8 = Rs 1,000 and actual mix costs 40 x 12 + 60 x 8 = Rs 960, so mix variance = 1,000 - 960 = Rs 40 Favourable.

q: Under activity-based costing, the machine set-up cost pool of a plant is Rs 1,80,000 and the total number of set-ups in the period is 900. A product requiring 180 set-ups will be assigned set-up cost of:

options.A: Rs 200

e: Set-up rate = 1,80,000 / 900 = Rs 200 per set-up, so the product is assigned 180 x Rs 200 = Rs 36,000.

q: The expected market price of a new product is Rs 1,200 per unit and the firm desires a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. The target cost of the product is:

options.A: Rs 960 per unit
options.B: Rs 1,000 per unit
options.C: Rs 240 per unit
options.D: Rs 1,440 per unit

e: Target cost = Expected price minus desired profit = 1,200 - 20 percent of 1,200 = 1,200 - 240 = Rs 960 per unit.

q: The primary object of cost audit is to verify that:

options.A: The financial statements give a true and fair view for shareholders
options.B: No tax has been evaded by the enterprise
options.C: The wages paid to workers agree with the muster roll
options.D: Cost accounts and cost records are correctly maintained and cost data are reliable for managerial and regulatory purposes

e: Cost audit verifies that cost accounts and records are properly maintained under the costing system and that cost data are accurate and reliable for management and regulatory use.

q: A component can be made in-house at a variable cost of Rs 52 per unit, or bought at Rs 58 per unit. If it is bought, the released capacity can earn a contribution of Rs 10 per unit on other work. For a requirement of 5,000 units, the correct decision and its effect are:

options.A: Make, saving Rs 30,000
options.B: Buy, because the effective cost of buying (Rs 48 per unit) is lower, saving Rs 20,000
options.C: Make, saving Rs 20,000
options.D: Remain indifferent, as the net difference is nil

e: Effective buy cost = Rs 58 - Rs 10 contribution from released capacity = Rs 48, versus make cost Rs 52, so buying saves (52 - 48) x 5,000 = Rs 20,000.

q: A firm with spare capacity receives a one-time special order for 6,000 units at Rs 68 per unit. The variable cost is Rs 60 per unit, but accepting the order requires special tooling costing Rs 30,000. The order should be:

options.A: Rejected, because the tooling cost makes it unprofitable
options.B: Accepted only if the price is raised to Rs 75 per unit
options.C: Rejected, because the price is below the normal selling price
options.D: Accepted, because it yields a net incremental gain of Rs 18,000

e: Incremental gain = 6,000 x (68 - 60) - 30,000 tooling = 48,000 - 30,000 = Rs 18,000 positive, and with spare capacity only variable cost is relevant, so the order is accepted.

q: Life-cycle costing is most useful to management at the design stage of a product because:

options.A: All costs of the product are incurred only during manufacture
options.B: It ignores the costs of servicing and disposal of the product
options.C: A large part of the total life-cycle cost is committed by design decisions, even though it is actually incurred later in production, use and disposal
options.D: It applies only to products with a life of more than ten years

e: Most life-cycle cost is locked in by design choices on materials and features, though incurred later in manufacture, use, servicing and disposal, so design is the stage to control total cost.

q: Cost-benefit analysis of a project, as distinct from a purely financial appraisal, is characterised by:

options.A: Comparing only the cash receipts and cash payments of the sponsoring authority
options.B: Ignoring all costs and benefits that cannot be expressed in money terms
options.C: Identifying and valuing, in money terms as far as possible, all costs and all benefits of the project to society as a whole over its life, and comparing the two
options.D: Comparing the capital cost of the project with the budget provision available for it

e: Cost-benefit analysis covers society as a whole, valuing all social costs and benefits in money terms as far as possible over the project life, unlike financial appraisal limited to the sponsor.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Financial appraisal of a project values its inputs and outputs at market prices and measures the return accruing to the investing authority itself.
2. Economic appraisal values inputs and outputs at economic (shadow) prices where market prices are distorted, and measures the net benefit accruing to the economy as a whole.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

e: Both statements are correct: financial appraisal uses market prices for the investing authority, while economic appraisal uses shadow prices and measures net benefit to the whole economy.

q: In sensitivity analysis, the 'switching value' of a project variable is:

options.A: The discount rate at which the project is switched from one year to another
options.B: The value which that variable would have to reach for the project's Net Present Value to become zero, that is, for the accept/reject decision to switch
options.C: The value of the variable in the first year of operation
options.D: The difference between the optimistic and pessimistic estimates of the variable

e: The switching value is the value a key variable must reach to make NPV exactly zero, so the accept decision switches to reject; it shows how much adverse change the project can bear.

q: Under the risk-adjusted discount rate method of handling risk in project appraisal:

options.A: A higher discount rate is applied to the cash flows of a riskier project, which reduces the present value of its distant inflows
options.B: The same risk-free rate is applied to all projects, whatever their risk
options.C: The cash flows of a riskier project are increased to allow for the risk
options.D: Risk is ignored once the payback period has been computed

e: The risk-adjusted discount rate raises the discount rate for riskier projects, which reduces the present value of distant and uncertain inflows and makes acceptance harder.

q: An enterprise has more independent projects with positive Net Present Value than its limited capital budget can finance. This situation of capital rationing calls for:

options.A: Accepting the projects in the order in which they were proposed
options.B: Rejecting all the projects, since funds are limited
options.C: Selecting the combination of projects that yields the highest total Net Present Value within the funds available
options.D: Accepting only the single largest project

e: Under capital rationing with indivisible limited funds, the aim is the feasible combination of positive NPV projects giving the highest total NPV within the budget.

q: The discount rate used in appraising a project represents, in essence:

options.A: The rate of depreciation of the assets created by the project
options.B: The opportunity cost of the capital employed, that is, the return foregone on the best alternative use of the same funds
options.C: The rate of inflation expected during the life of the project
options.D: The dividend rate payable on the capital-at-charge

e: The discount rate is the opportunity cost of capital - the return sacrificed on the best alternative use of the same funds - which is why future flows are discounted at it.

q: A project requires an initial investment of Rs 12,00,000 and has a Net Present Value of (+) Rs 1,80,000. Its Profitability Index is:
What is the present value of an annuity of Rs 1,50,000 receivable at the end of each of the next 4 years, discounted at 10% (cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% = 3.170)?
e: Present value of annuity = Rs 1,50,000 x 3.170 = Rs 4,75,500.

q: The present value of Rs 2,50,000 receivable at the end of 2 years, at a discount rate of 10% (present value factor for Year 2 = 0.826), is:
e: Present value = Rs 2,50,000 x 0.826 = Rs 2,06,500.

q: Rs 2,00,000 is invested today at a compound interest (discount) rate of 10% per annum. Its value at the end of 2 years (future value factor for 2 years at 10% = 1.21) will be:
e: Future value = Rs 2,00,000 x 1.21 = Rs 2,42,000.

q: A project costing Rs 5,00,000 has discounted (present) values of cash inflows of Rs 1,50,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,50,000 in Year 2 and Rs 3,00,000 in Year 3. Its discounted payback period is:

options.A: 2 years and 8 months
options.B: 2 years and 6 months
options.C: 3 years
options.D: 2 years and 3 months

e: Cumulative discounted inflows are Rs 1,50,000 in Year 1 and Rs 3,00,000 by Year 2; the balance Rs 2,00,000 of the Rs 5,00,000 cost needs 2,00,000/3,00,000 = 8 months of Year 3, so discounted payback is 2 years 8 months.

q: A project has a Profitability Index of 1.4 and requires an initial investment of Rs 8,00,000. Its Net Present Value is:
At a discount rate of 12%, a project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 9,000, and at a discount rate of 18% it is (-) Rs 6,000. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: IRR = 12 percent + 9,000 / (9,000 + 6,000) x (18 - 12) percent = 12 + 0.6 x 6 = 15.6 percent by interpolation.

q: The Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return methods may rank two mutually exclusive projects differently mainly because of differences between the projects in:

options.A: The currency in which their cash flows are expressed
options.B: The scale (size) of investment and the timing (pattern) of their cash flows, together with the different reinvestment assumptions of the two methods
options.C: The names given to the projects in the works programme
options.D: The accounting year in which they are sanctioned

e: NPV and IRR can conflict for mutually exclusive projects because of different investment scale and cash-flow timing, and because IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR while NPV assumes the cost of capital.

q: A project whose cash flows change sign more than once during its life (for example, an inflow followed by a large restoration outlay) may give rise to:

options.A: Multiple internal rates of return, making the IRR criterion ambiguous for such a project
options.B: A negative payback period
options.C: A Profitability Index of exactly zero
options.D: No cash flow in the final year

e: Each sign change can produce another root of the NPV equation, so non-conventional cash flows with later outflows can give multiple IRRs and the IRR rule becomes ambiguous.

q: Two mutually exclusive machines have different economic lives. The Net Present Value of one machine is Rs 1,10,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 2.5. Its Equivalent Annual Annuity (equivalent annual benefit) is:
e: Equivalent Annual Annuity = NPV / annuity factor = 1,10,000 / 2.5 = Rs 44,000 per year, used to compare projects of unequal lives.

q: A new machine costs Rs 5,60,000. The old machine it will replace can be sold immediately for Rs 90,000. The net (incremental) initial cash outlay on the replacement is:
e: Net initial outlay = Cost of new machine minus disposal proceeds of old machine = 5,60,000 - 90,000 = Rs 4,70,000.

q: In a machine replacement decision, the book value of the existing machine is generally irrelevant to the decision (except for any tax or disposal effect) because it is:

options.A: Always equal to its current realisable value
options.B: A sunk cost representing capital already spent, which cannot be recovered by either alternative
options.C: A future cash outflow under both alternatives
options.D: Included in the price of the new machine

e: Book value is a sunk cost - capital already spent and unrecoverable under either alternative - so only future incremental cash flows, plus any tax or disposal effect, are relevant.

q: In appraising a new project, an amount already spent on a preliminary survey for that very project in an earlier year should be treated as:

options.A: A cash outflow of the project in its first year
options.B: A part of the initial investment of the project
options.C: A sunk cost, excluded from the project's cash flows, since it will remain spent whether or not the project is now accepted
options.D: A deduction from the project's earnings in the final year

e: Money already spent on the survey stays spent whether the project proceeds or not, so it is a sunk cost and is excluded from the incremental cash flows of the appraisal.

q: The earnings projected in the financial justification of a new railway line rest principally on traffic projections, under which the traffic expected on the new line is made up of:

options.A: Only the traffic already moving on the existing lines of the railway
options.B: Only the traffic carried in the first year of operation
options.C: Originating traffic, traffic diverted from existing routes or modes, and newly generated (developed) traffic
options.D: Only the coaching traffic expected on the line

e: Traffic projections for a new line comprise originating traffic, traffic diverted from existing routes or other modes, and newly generated or developed traffic induced by the line.
